title: Energetic Costs of Subspace Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction acts as an entropy pump, transferring noise-induced uncertainty from a protected quantum system into syndrome information stored in an auxiliary memory. Repeated operation requires this memory to be cleared which unavoidably contributes to the energetic cost of error correction. Here, we characterise this contribution for subspace quantum error-correcting codes and identify how it depends on the joint structure of the code, the noise, and the representation of the retained syndrome information. Starting from the Knill-Laflamme conditions, we construct an effective syndrome state whose von Neumann entropy sets a lower bound on the ideal work required to maintain a reusable syndrome register. Projective syndrome readout generally generates additional entropy, and we quantify the resulting gap through measurement inefficiency. We then specialise to stabiliser codes under independent local Pauli noise and analyse two classical levels of syndrome representation. At the level of abstract error labels, degeneracies among single-qubit errors reduce the leading-order entropy of processed recovery labels. At the parity-check level, lower-weight checks reduce the marginal entropy generated by individual measurement outcomes in the low-noise regime. We identify the additional burden associated with retaining and separately erasing these outcomes as a bit-level inefficiency, and illustrate both costs for the five-qubit, Steane, generalised Shor, and rotated surface codes. Our results establish a hierarchy of syndrome-memory energetic costs and identify the code, noise, and measurement structures that control the ideal thermodynamic burden of subspace quantum error correction.

title: Beyond BLEU: A Case for Redefining Sign Language Translation Benchmarks
abstract: BLEU-4 is the standard metric for evaluating sign language translation (SLT), but spoken-language metrics may not adequately reflect sign language proficiency. The multimodal, low-resource context of SLT allows models to exploit spurious correlations and spoken-language priors, rather than learning stronger sign representations. In this paper, we evaluate the relationship between spatio-temporal understanding and BLEU-4 across six SLT models on Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily, showing that gains in BLEU-4 are not on their own evidence of better sign language understanding. This work introduces an alternative inspired by language-learning assessment, using an open-weight-LLM QA protocol that measures salient content preservation. It aligns more closely with human rankings and is six to seven times more paraphrase-invariant than BLEU-4. Applied to SLT, this protocol targets content transfer, is more robust to train-test overlap, and gives a different picture of the field: the five gloss-free systems are largely within noise of one another on Phoenix-2014T, while the gloss-supervised system stands 9.3 points higher, a gap invisible to BLEU-4.

title: Scaling Bimanual Household Manipulation from 1,500 hours of Demonstrations to On-Policy Corrections
abstract: Learning generalist policies for robust bimanual manipulation is bottlenecked by the scarcity of high quality large scale human demonstration data. In this work, we release 1,500 hours of diverse bimanual manipulation demonstrations covering everyday household tasks, and use this comprehensive corpus to train XR-2, a powerful vision-language-action (VLA) model. Enabled by a purpose built high throughput data pipeline and a carefully designed multi stage training paradigm, XR-2 attains strong manipulation performance in our systematic experiments while retaining favorable training efficiency and high data utilization. We further study two critical scaling axes: varying the amount of expert demonstration data, and post training on DAgger correction data from real time human interventions. In both settings, task success rate improves steadily over the data ranges we probe, exhibiting a clear consistent scaling trend at our current data scale. These results validate both the learning capacity of XR-2 and the promising scaling properties of the released dataset, which we open source to support reproducible research on bimanual robot manipulation learning.

title: Mathematical Foundations and Applications in Machine Learning
abstract: Machine learning has developed into a powerful tool for forecasting and drawing inferences from large amounts of information. Machine learning algorithms are based on mathematical concepts to build models, discover patterns and generate accurate predictions. This paper investigates the application of mathematics in various machine learning models and methods. It illustrates how several mathematical fields work together to develop useful machine learning methods. Creating an algorithm that suggests a model that can learn from data and make predictions. It is used to understand why a model is superior to another and why something works. An inherent mathematical prerequisite is machine learning. Calculus, probability, linear algebra and statistics all work together to power machine learning.

title: Adaptive Feature Selection via Generative Adversarial Networks (FGAN)
abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to feature selection utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We propose a novel framework where a GAN learns to generate synthetic feature sets, dynamically adjusting feature selection based on the inherent variability within the training data. The system aims to enhance model generalization by proactively addressing data noise and uncertainty, resulting in improved predictive performance. This research introduces a robust and adaptable feature selection method that addresses limitations of traditional techniques.

title: Self-Adaptive Geometric Methods for Deep Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive geometric method for deep learning, designed to dynamically adjust geometric structures based on input data. Traditional deep learning frameworks often employ static representations, limiting the model's flexibility and potentially hindering optimization. This research proposes a method that iteratively refines the geometric representation of the input data, leading to improved accuracy and computational efficiency. The core mechanism involves a self-organizing process that continuously updates geometric parameters, resulting in a more robust and adaptable model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of experiments evaluating its performance on diverse deep learning tasks. The paper highlights the potential of this method to address limitations of existing deep learning architectures.

title: 基于动态自适应模型的参数调整
abstract: This paper introduces a novel parameter adjustment method for machine learning models based on dynamic adaptive models. Traditional parameter adjustment methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their ability to effectively adapt to data variations and improve prediction accuracy. The proposed method employs a dynamic self-adaptive model, learning model parameter characteristics to automatically adjust them, thereby mitigating the limitations of fixed parameter models. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through extensive experiments across several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing techniques. The core mechanism focuses on learning a self-adaptation function that governs parameter updates, resulting in more robust and adaptable models.

title: A Lower Bound on Energy Cost per Logical-Qubit Operation in Surface-Code Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Surface-code quantum error correction (QEC) is pivotal for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but its energy efficiency remains underexplored. This work derives a practical lower bound on the energy cost per logical-qubit operation, accounting for gate-fidelity decay's impact on code distance and physical-qubit overhead. By modeling the energy consumption of gate operations and error correction, we express the total cost as $ E = (E_g N_g + E_c N_c)/N_l $, where $ E_g $, $ E_c $, $ N_g $, $ N_c $, and $ N_l $ represent gate and physical-qubit energy costs, gate counts, physical-qubit counts, and logical qubit counts, respectively. Gate-fidelity decay increases the required code distance $ d $, scaling $ N_c $ and thus $ E $. We propose normalizing computational cost in joules per logical-qubit operation (JPCUB), isolating logical work from error-correction overhead. Quantitative predictions for $ E_g $, $ E_c $, and $ N_c $ remain [to verify], but the functional dependence on $ d $ and gate fidelities is established. This framework informs energy-efficient QEC design and benchmarks. ## 1. Introduction Surface codes enable fault-tolerant quantum computation by encoding logical qubits in a 2D lattice of physical qubits, correcting errors through syndrome measurements. However, the energy cost per logical operation—critical for scalability—remains poorly quantified. While theoretical foundations exist (Raussendorf & Terhal, 2006; Kitaev, 2003), prior work focuses on error-correction thresholds rather than energy efficiency. Here, we address this gap by deriving a lower bound on energy cost, considering how gate-fidelity decay necessitates larger code distances $ d $, increasing physical-qubit overhead $ N_c $. This analysis connects to the joules-per-compute (JPCUB) benchmark, advocating for energy normalization per logical qubit to disentangle computational work from error-correction costs. ## 2. title: Quantum Adaptive Path Optimization
abstract: Quantum adaptive path optimization is a novel approach to algorithm optimization within the context of quantum computation. This paper proposes a quantum path optimization strategy that dynamically adjusts quantum path parameters to enhance algorithmic efficiency and reduce computational costs. The core mechanism utilizes quantum state evolution to iteratively refine and optimize the path, resulting in improved performance compared to traditional optimization techniques. This approach offers a promising pathway toward more efficient and cost-effective quantum algorithm design. The study explores the potential of this method through theoretical analysis and preliminary implementation on a simplified quantum circuit.

title: Dynamically Reconfigurable Neural Networks via Genetic Programming
abstract: This paper investigates the limitations of traditional static neural networks in dynamic and unpredictable environments. The core argument is presented: static neural networks lack the inherent flexibility required to adapt effectively to evolving conditions. To address this deficiency, a novel approach is proposed – dynamically reconfigurable neural networks achieved through the application of genetic programming. This methodology leverages evolutionary algorithms to continuously optimize the network's architecture and weight parameters in real-time, responding directly to feedback from the environment. The system's self-reconfiguring capability is demonstrated through a theoretical framework, detailing the core mechanisms and potential benefits. Key components include a fitness function to evaluate network performance, a genetic operator set for architectural and weight modification, and a feedback loop for environmental interaction. The paper outlines the theoretical foundations and provides a roadmap for implementing such a system, highlighting its potential to overcome the rigidity associated with conventional neural network designs. This approach offers a pathway toward more robust and adaptable artificial intelligence systems.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis with Hierarchical Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neuro-symbolic approach to program synthesis, leveraging the strengths of both neural networks and Bayesian Networks within a hierarchical framework. The core challenge in program synthesis, particularly for complex tasks involving hierarchical reasoning, is addressed by combining pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks with probabilistic reasoning of Bayesian Networks. The proposed system learns data patterns and simultaneously extracts underlying logical relationships, resulting in the generation of more sophisticated and, crucially, explainable programs. The hierarchical structure allows for the decomposition of complex problems into smaller, more manageable sub-problems, each addressed by a separate level of the Bayesian Network. This approach offers a significant advancement over existing program synthesis techniques by enabling the creation of programs capable of representing and executing intricate, nested logical rules. The system's architecture and learning process are detailed, demonstrating its potential for tackling complex programming challenges where traditional methods fall short.

title: Quantum-Accelerated Constraint Satisfaction for Large-Scale Problems
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing to significantly accelerate constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) on large-scale datasets. Current CSP solvers often struggle with scalability due to computational complexity. We propose a novel quantum algorithm for CSP solving, focusing on quantum parallelism to enhance search and constraint evaluation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and preliminary experiments on a benchmark CSP dataset. The core claim is that quantum-accelerated CSP solvers can offer a substantial improvement in performance compared to classical methods, particularly for large-scale problems.

title: Temporal Graph Embedding with Causality-Aware Relational Dynamics
abstract: Graph embedding techniques have achieved remarkable success in representing nodes and relationships within graphs for downstream tasks. However, a significant limitation remains when dealing with dynamic graphs, where nodes and their connections evolve over time. Existing methods often treat temporal information as a simple sequence of static graph snapshots, failing to capture the underlying causal dynamics and the sequential dependencies between nodes. This paper introduces a novel temporal graph embedding approach that explicitly incorporates causality and temporal dynamics. We construct a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to represent the causal relationships within the graph, and then utilize a recurrent neural network (RNN) to model the evolution of node embeddings based on this DAG. This methodology allows us to capture the influence of past events on current states while maintaining a structured representation of the graph. The core idea is to leverage the DAG to guide the RNN's state updates, ensuring that the temporal evolution of node embeddings is consistent with the causal structure. The resulting embeddings effectively represent the dynamic behavior of the graph, improving performance in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. The primary contribution is a framework for temporal graph embedding that integrates causality and temporal dynamics, offering a more robust and accurate representation of evolving graph systems.

title: ##基于时间扭曲的因果推理模型
abstract: This paper introduces a novel causal inference model that leverages the concept of "time distortion" to enhance the identification and processing of temporal dependencies within causal relationships. The model represents time as a variable dimension, incorporating a "time distortion" parameter to simulate delays, overlaps, and influences between events. This distortion dynamically adjusts the connection strength between nodes, facilitating temporal reasoning. The core claim is that simulating time distortion provides a more effective approach to causal inference by acknowledging and modeling the complexities of time-dependent relationships. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to improve accuracy in causal reasoning scenarios where traditional methods often fall short due to their assumption of absolute time. The model utilizes a graph-based representation of causal relationships and incorporates time-dependent weighting to prioritize causal links based on temporal proximity and distortion levels. The theoretical framework is presented, followed by a discussion of the model's key components and potential applications.

title: Computational Semantics for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: This paper proposes a novel computational semantic framework designed to address the challenges of natural language understanding (NLU) by moving beyond traditional symbolic approaches. The core idea is to represent the meaning of natural language sentences using a dynamic logic system augmented with probabilistic reasoning. This allows for the capture of contextual nuances and inference processes inherent in human language comprehension. The framework utilizes dynamic logic to model the evolution of meaning over time and context, while probabilistic reasoning provides a mechanism for handling uncertainty and ambiguity. title: Algorithmic Transparency via Computational Traceability
abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various domains, yet their "black box" nature poses significant challenges to trust, interpretability, and accountability. This research addresses this issue by proposing a novel system for achieving algorithmic transparency through detailed computational traceability. The system meticulously captures and represents the entire execution process of a deep learning model, encompassing intermediate activations, gradient flows during training, and the decision pathways leading to a specific output. This approach moves beyond simple model explanations and provides a granular, verifiable record of the model's internal workings. The core claim is that this level of detail is crucial for fostering trust and facilitating a deeper understanding of these complex systems. The system's architecture is described, along with the key components and their functionalities. Finally, potential applications and future research directions are discussed, highlighting the transformative impact of computational traceability on the field of deep learning.

title: Quantum Neural Networks: Topology Optimization of Neuronal Connections
abstract: This paper investigates the application of topology optimization techniques to enhance the performance of quantum neural networks (QNNs). Traditional QNN architectures often suffer from inefficiencies in information processing due to suboptimal connections between neurons. This work proposes a novel approach utilizing topology optimization algorithms to dynamically adjust the connectivity topology within a QNN, aiming to maximize computational capacity and efficiency. The core claim is that optimizing the neuronal connection topology is a key factor in improving QNN performance. The proposed mechanism involves the iterative application of a topology optimization algorithm, which iteratively modifies the network's connectivity structure based on a defined objective function. The results demonstrate the potential of this method to significantly improve QNN performance, offering a pathway to more powerful and efficient quantum computing architectures. The specific objective function utilized focuses on maximizing the fidelity of quantum state transformations while minimizing the number of connections, representing a novel approach to QNN design. Further exploration will involve investigating different optimization algorithms and network architectures to fully realize the potential of this topology-optimized QNN design.

title: Quantum Privacy Preservation Communication Protocol Based on Quantum Coherence Collapse
abstract: This paper proposes a novel quantum communication protocol designed for privacy preservation, leveraging the phenomenon of quantum coherence collapse. The core idea is to utilize quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols and strategically introduce coherence collapse operations during transmission, effectively hindering an eavesdropper's ability to access the key. Unlike existing QKD protocols that predominantly rely on quantum entanglement, this approach exploits the unique characteristics of quantum coherence collapse. We outline the protocol's architecture, detailing the key steps involved in key generation and distribution, focusing on the precise implementation of the coherence collapse mechanism. The protocol's security analysis demonstrates its potential to provide robust privacy protection against various eavesdropping attacks. Mathematical formulations are presented to rigorously describe the protocol's operations and security properties. The primary goal is to present a fundamentally different approach to quantum privacy preservation, offering a potentially more secure and efficient solution compared to entanglement-based QKD.

title: Title: Geometric Language for Formalizing Uncertainty in Neural Networks
abstract: Neural networks, while achieving remarkable results, often struggle with uncertainty. Current approaches often rely on approximations and heuristics, which can lead to instability and unreliable predictions. This paper proposes a novel geometric language for formalizing uncertainty within neural networks, aiming to create more robust and reliable models. We introduce a grammar based on Bayesian inference and Monte Carlo simulation, allowing for explicit representation of probabilistic relationships and uncertainty quantification. The core mechanism involves defining a geometric representation of the network's parameters and activations, enabling the construction of probabilistic models and analysis. This approach offers a pathway toward enhanced uncertainty management, potentially leading to improved model generalization and decision-making. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this language through a simplified illustrative example, showcasing its ability to capture and quantify uncertainty in a basic neural network model.

Our approach integrates neural networks and symbolic reasoning to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters through iterative optimization, resulting in enhanced algorithm efficiency and robustness. We detail the core mechanism, outlining the interplay between neural networks and symbolic representations, and highlight the benefits of this adaptive approach. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's performance evaluation and potential applications.

title: Title: Self-Organizing Fractal Networks with Constraint Feedback
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to self-organizing fractal networks, leveraging a Constraint Feedback Loop to guide the formation of intricate patterns. We introduce a neural network architecture designed to foster emergent properties within a constrained environment, producing highly efficient and adaptable computational structures. The core mechanism centers on this Constraint Feedback Loop, which dynamically adjusts the network's output based on the fractal's self-generated shape, enabling self-replication and complex generation. We explore the potential applications of these networks in data compression and material science, demonstrating the effectiveness of this method in producing novel fractal structures.

Traditional quantum computing approaches often require manual parameter tuning, limiting the algorithm's adaptability. Our proposed algorithm leverages the inherent properties of quantum fields to automatically optimize quantum computation, offering a significant advancement in parameter space exploration and algorithm design. We explore the core mechanism of the algorithm, focusing on the use of quantum fields to iteratively refine and adjust parameters to maximize a predefined objective function. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, its performance evaluation, and potential applications in quantum optimization and exploration.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Artificial Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired optimization techniques to accelerate the training of deep learning models. The core concept revolves around leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to guide the optimization process, specifically through the creation of a "quantum-state approximation" that reduces computational complexity. We propose a novel method that utilizes quantum phenomena to enhance feature selection, ultimately aiming to improve the training speed and performance of deep neural networks. The research explores the potential benefits of this approach, focusing on addressing the computational bottlenecks inherent in deep learning. The paper presents a detailed theoretical analysis and a preliminary implementation of the proposed optimization method.

title: 基于自适应神经网络的生态系统建模
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for ecosystem modeling based on adaptive neural networks. Traditional ecosystem models often rely on manual parameter adjustment, limiting the model's flexibility and hindering accurate representation of complex ecological dynamics. This work introduces an adaptive neural network (ANN) architecture that dynamically adjusts model parameters based on observed data, enabling automated parameter optimization and improved predictive capabilities. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy through simulated ecosystem evolution, showcasing its ability to accurately model and respond to environmental changes. The core mechanism focuses on an ANN that learns to represent the system's state and dynamics, facilitating a more robust and adaptive modeling approach. The framework's key contribution lies in its ability to achieve a higher degree of environmental responsiveness and facilitates a more streamlined approach to ecosystem analysis and prediction.

abstract: Quantum Machine Learning aims to leverage the unique properties of quantum mechanics to revolutionize artificial intelligence. This paper introduces a novel adaptive gradient descent algorithm incorporating quantum entanglement and superposition, promising significant acceleration in training complex models and improved accuracy. The core claim centers on the potential for quantum-enhanced gradient descent, leading to breakthroughs in machine learning applications. This work explores the theoretical underpinnings and potential practical implications of this innovative approach.

title: Adaptive Optimization Algorithm Based on Quantum Error Correction
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive optimization algorithm based on quantum error correction, designed to dynamically adjust optimization strategies in response to noise and errors during computation. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their adaptability to complex environments. Leveraging quantum mechanics, specifically the entanglement and superposition of quantum states, we propose a novel approach that allows the algorithm to continuously refine its optimization path and achieve improved precision. The core mechanism involves quantum state manipulation, error correction, and dynamic adjustment of optimization parameters based on the observed noise and errors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through simulations, illustrating its ability to enhance solution accuracy and robustness compared to conventional optimization techniques. The paper also discusses the potential advantages and challenges associated with this approach, highlighting the significance of quantum error correction in optimizing complex computational systems.

title: L’usage du calcul quantique en finance La perspective d’un institut académique à l’interface entre technologies et usages
abstract: Dans cet article, nous analysons l’impact potentiel du calcul quantique sur la finance du point de vue d’un institut académique positionné à l’interface entre technologies et usages. Nous défendons l’idée que le quantique constitue un bien public, dont les implications dépassent le seul cadre technologique et nécessitent une appropriation par les décideurs économiques. Après avoir souligné l’importance d’une pédagogie adaptée pour rendre ces concepts accessibles aux non-physiciens, nous proposons une taxonomie des principaux algorithmes quantiques pertinents pour la finance : optimisation, algèbre linéaire, Monte Carlo et apprentissage automatique. Ces approches trouvent des applications naturelles dans l’optimisation de portefeuille, la gestion du risque et le pricing de produits dérivés. Enfin, nous mettons en perspective la maturité actuelle du domaine : malgré des avancées significatives, les bénéfices opérationnels restent limités à court terme, tandis que les véritables ruptures sont attendues avec l’émergence de machines quantiques tolérantes aux fautes.

title: A Multi-Indicator Concentration Index for Primary-Care Reimbursement Analytics: Evidence from the Albanian Health-Insurance System
abstract: Background: Public payers must regularly decide which prescribers to look at more closely, with records covering thousands of doctors per quarter and review capacity for only a fraction. How that choice is made bears on equitable access to reimbursed medicines as well as on public funds. Methods: We propose a multi-indicator concentration index scoring each prescriber 0–100 as the sum of nine weighted sub-scores, each measuring the doctor’s deviation from their primary-care centre median on one indicator from the payer’s routine quarterly report; eight are computable from a single quarter. Every score decomposes into named components. The index measures the concentration of indicators above the peer profile, not an estimated probability of misconduct. It is a screening tool for prioritising documentary review. We demonstrate it on one quarter of anonymised data from 335 doctors in 30 Albanian primary-care centres. Results: The eight active sub-scores are mostly weakly correlated (mean |r|=0.28), the two exceptions each pairing a case count with its financial effect. Rankings are robust to alternative weights (Spearman ρ between 0.93 and 0.98), to collapsing those pairs (ρ≥0.98), and to pooling the smallest centres against a shared comparator (ρ=0.95). Against three machine-learning anomaly detectors and two simpler screens, the index selects a different top cohort: doctors whose spending is only moderately raised, but whose new-case and therapy-change counts exceed three times the centre median. In an internal concordance check, two co-author reviewers blinded to the score rated 60 cases sampled partly by index rank; they agreed with each other (Cohen’s κ=0.87, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.00), and the index’s ranking against their consensus gives an AUC of 0.88 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.97). Conclusions: The index gives clinical-administrative reviewers a reproducible, explainable priority order consistent with senior expert judgement on the same indicators. Because no review outcomes are linked to the records and the window is a single quarter, it is supported as a prioritisation tool, not a validated predictor of inappropriate reimbursement; multi-quarter and outcome-linked evaluation are the next steps.

title: DSSR-3D: Decoupled Reasoning for View-Dependent Referring in 3D Gaussians
abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have enabled open-vocabulary and referring segmentation by distilling semantic knowledge from 2D foundation models into 3D representations. However, existing referring fields embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. We propose DSSR-3D, an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields, formalized as two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - such that any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation, requiring no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no reliance on discrete geometric proxies such as bounding boxes. We instantiate the two interfaces with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step, and show they transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. We further propose ViewRef-GS, a benchmark isolating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, evaluated jointly with an augmented Ref-LERF to provide a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding. Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field

title: A Repeated-Measurement Study for Cultural Analytics of English Song Lyrics Using Five Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate cultural texts at scales that are impractical for human coders. However, before their outputs are treated as measurements of latent social constructs, it is necessary to establish whether those measurements are reliable. This study evaluates five LLMs as zero-shot annotators of four social constructs expressed in English song lyrics: self-esteem, self-control, seeking belonging, and seeking recognition. Using repeated annotations of a large lyric corpus, we examine three properties of LLM-based measurement: consistency across repeated runs, convergence across models, and transferability of consensus labels to supervised classification. The findings show that LLM-based measurement is not uniformly reliable across constructs. Self-esteem exhibits the strongest repeated-measurement reliability across models, while seeking recognition is generally less stable; self-control and seeking belonging show intermediate but model-dependent reliability. Downstream classification further indicates that consensus LLM labels contain learnable signal, although transferability does not itself establish construct validity. Repeated-measurement stability and cross-model convergence should therefore be reported before LLM annotations are treated as scalable measurements in cultural analytics.

title: Tree species mapping in Denmark: A comparison of spectral-temporal features with geospatial foundation model embeddings
abstract: We map tree species across Denmark using National Forest Inventory plots and EO data, while evaluating the potential of foundation models for large-scale forest characterization. We compare two alternative input representations for tree species classification: (i) manually engineered spectral-temporal features (STF) derived from multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations, and (ii) embeddings generated by the EO FMs TESSERA and AlphaEarth. Both representations are complemented with canopy height information. Random forest, XGBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers are evaluated for all input representations, with separate assessments for pure and mixed forest stands. The STF-based MLP achieves the highest classification performance, yielding macro F1 scores of 0.843 and 0.653 for pure and mixed stands, respectively. The MLP trained on TESSERA embeddings delivers competitive performance for pure stands, achieving results within 1.1 percentage points of the best-performing model. TESSERA consistently outperforms STF-based models when fewer than approximately 25% of training plots are available, demonstrating a substantial advantage under limited training data. Multi-year observations systematically improve classification accuracy relative to single-year inputs, while ablation experiments reveal the complementary contributions of Sentinel-1 backscatter, spectral indices, and canopy height data. The best-performing model is subsequently applied at the national scale to generate a 10 m tree species map of Denmark. Area-adjusted validation indicates an overall map accuracy of 79.9%. The resulting map, released as an open-access product, is the first high-resolution national tree species map of Denmark and provides a valuable resource for forest monitoring, ecological research, and land management applications.

Multi-year observations systematically improve classification accuracy relative to single-year inputs, while ablation experiments reveal the complementary contributions of Sentinel-1 backscatter, spectral indices, and canopy height data. The best-performing model is subsequently applied at the national scale to generate a 10 m tree species map of Denmark. Area-adjusted validation indicates an overall map accuracy of 79.9%. The resulting map, released as an open-access product, is the first high-resolution national tree species map of Denmark and provides a valuable resource for forest monitoring, ecological research, and land management applications.

title: RAFT: A Real-World Few-Shot Text Classification Benchmark
abstract: Large pre-trained language models have shown promise for few-shot learning, completing text-based tasks given only a few task-specific examples. Will models soon solve classification tasks that have so far been reserved for human research assistants? Existing benchmarks are not designed to measure progress in applied settings, and so don't directly answer this question. The RAFT benchmark (Real-world Annotated Few-shot Tasks) focuses on naturally occurring tasks and uses an evaluation setup that mirrors deployment. Baseline evaluations on RAFT reveal areas current techniques struggle with: reasoning over long texts and tasks with many classes. Human baselines show that some classification tasks are difficult for non-expert humans, reflecting that real-world value sometimes depends on domain expertise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design through a series of simulations, showcasing enhanced convergence speed and improved performance on a challenging reinforcement learning task. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications and future directions of this research.

title: Self-Supervised Learning via Predictive State Transitions in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to self-supervised learning (SSL) that leverages the inherent predictability of state transitions within complex systems. The core idea is to train a model to forecast the future state of a system, given its past and current state. This approach frames the complex system's dynamics as a generative process, enabling the model to learn representations directly from the underlying data without explicit labels. We demonstrate the potential of this method across diverse complex systems, including biological networks and climate models. The central contribution lies in the formulation of a predictive learning objective that captures the sequential dependencies critical to understanding system behavior. We outline the key components of the framework, including the model architecture, training procedure, and evaluation metrics. The results suggest that this self-supervised method can effectively learn meaningful representations and potentially improve downstream tasks that require an understanding of system dynamics. The core of the method is to build a model that can predict state transitions, thereby learning the underlying rules of the system. This is achieved through a predictive state transition objective.

title: Quantum Adaptive Algorithm Parameter Optimization
abstract: Quantum adaptive algorithms offer the potential for significant speedups in complex computations, particularly in areas like quantum chemistry and materials science. However, achieving optimal performance often requires careful optimization of quantum parameters, a task that can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel quantum adaptive algorithm that dynamically adjusts quantum parameters to optimize algorithm efficiency and accuracy, thereby reducing computational costs. We propose a method centered around a feedback loop that continuously monitors and adjusts the parameters based on the algorithm's output, leading to a more robust and adaptable optimization strategy. The core mechanism leverages a dynamic parameter tuning process to achieve this. This research explores the potential of this approach in tackling specific challenges within quantum algorithm design and provides a framework for future development. The key innovation lies in the continuous feedback loop that dynamically adjusts parameters, resulting in a more efficient and accurate algorithm.

title: Quantum Annealing Algorithm Optimization and Application
abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) is a promising quantum computing paradigm for solving optimization problems. However, the performance of QA is often limited by issues such as slow convergence rates and sensitivity to parameter settings. This paper presents a novel optimization method designed to address these limitations. The approach introduces refined parameters and an adaptive strategy to enhance the algorithm's convergence speed and solution accuracy. We explore the application of this optimized QA method to complex problems, demonstrating its potential for improved performance. The core of the optimization lies in modifying the annealing schedule and incorporating a dynamic adjustment of the magnetic field strength, denoted as $H(t)$, where $t$ represents time. The objective function to be minimized is typically represented as $E[s]$, where $s$ is the state vector of the quantum annealer. We introduce a variance reduction technique, denoted as $\sigma(t)$, which is dynamically adjusted based on the error estimates of the current state. The overall optimization process can be summarized as: $\min_{s} E[s] \quad \text{subject to} \quad \frac{dS}{dt} = - \beta(t) E[s] - \gamma(t) H(t)s$ where $\beta(t)$ is the annealing rate and $\gamma(t)$ is the magnetic field strength. The adaptive strategy involves updating $\beta(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ based on the error in the current solution, aiming to reduce the variance $\sigma(t)$ and improve the convergence. The theoretical analysis suggests that this approach can significantly reduce the computational cost and improve the solution quality compared to traditional QA methods. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of different parameter settings on the algorithm's performance, highlighting the importance of careful tuning for optimal results. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in solution quality and convergence speed across various benchmark problems.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning with Latent Time Scales
abstract: This paper introduces a novel hierarchical Bayesian deep learning framework designed to effectively capture long-range dependencies in temporal data. The core challenge in standard Bayesian deep learning lies in the difficulty of inference within high-dimensional latent spaces, hindering the model's ability to represent and learn correlations across extended time periods. Our approach addresses this limitation by incorporating latent time scales, creating a hierarchical structure where each layer learns to represent data at different temporal resolutions. This allows for a more efficient and accurate representation of temporal dependencies, leading to improved performance in tasks involving time series analysis and forecasting. We outline the key components of the framework, including the Bayesian inference process, the definition of latent time scales, and the architecture of the hierarchical deep learning model. The proposed method demonstrates the potential to overcome the limitations of traditional approaches and offers a promising direction for future research in temporal data modeling.

title: Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Graph Embedding
abstract: Learning effective graph embeddings from limited data, a scenario often encountered in real-world applications, presents a substantial challenge in graph representation learning. Traditional graph embedding methods typically require large datasets for training, leading to poor performance when only a few labeled examples are available. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to address this problem. Specifically, we train a meta-learning model that learns to quickly adapt to new graph embedding tasks with minimal labeled data. The core idea is to learn a meta-learner that can efficiently update its parameters based on a small number of examples, enabling rapid adaptation to diverse graph structures and tasks. We formulate the problem as a few-shot learning scenario, where the meta-learner learns to generalize across different graph embedding tasks. The performance of our approach is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in learning high-quality graph embeddings from limited data. The key contribution of this work lies in the application of meta-learning techniques to graph embedding, offering a promising solution for scenarios where data scarcity is a major constraint.

title: Symbolic Regression with Constraint Satisfaction Programming
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover mathematical equations from data. However, its performance suffers when dealing with complex constraints or high-dimensional data, leading to computationally expensive and often unproductive searches. This work proposes a novel approach that integrates symbolic regression with constraint satisfaction programming (CSP). The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both techniques: symbolic regression's ability to generate expressive mathematical models, and CSP's robust method for efficiently finding solutions that adhere to a set of constraints. We introduce a framework where the symbolic regression process is guided by a CSP engine, enabling the system to explore a constrained solution space. This approach significantly reduces the search space, improving the efficiency and accuracy of symbolic regression, particularly when dealing with complex relationships and limitations. The primary contribution is a novel method for enhancing symbolic regression's capability to address real-world scenarios characterized by intricate constraints and data complexities.

title: Quantum-Inspired Neural Networks with Adaptive Graph Structures
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to neural network design, termed Quantum-Inspired Neural Networks (QINNs) with Adaptive Graph Structures. The core idea is to leverage the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics – specifically superposition and entanglement – to create a network architecture that exhibits enhanced information processing capabilities. Traditional neural networks often struggle with complex, non-linear relationships and can suffer from vanishing gradients during training. QINNs address these limitations by employing dynamically evolving graph structures that mimic the interconnectedness and efficient information transfer observed in quantum systems. The network architecture is designed to represent data through a superposition of states, allowing for the exploration of multiple solution paths simultaneously. Furthermore, adaptive graph structures, inspired by entanglement, facilitate the correlation of information between nodes, significantly improving the network's ability to capture intricate patterns. This approach represents a significant departure from simply using quantum concepts as an inspirational element; it's a fundamental integration of quantum principles into the neural network design, leading to potentially superior performance in tasks demanding high computational efficiency and pattern recognition accuracy. The paper outlines the theoretical framework, the proposed architecture, and discusses the potential benefits and future research directions.

title: Quantum Security Proofs Based on Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper presents a theoretical framework for demonstrating the security of quantum algorithms leveraging the phenomenon of quantum decoherence. We explore the vulnerability of quantum algorithms to external disturbances, arguing that decoherence fundamentally undermines their computational advantage. Our core claim is that by precisely quantifying decoherence effects and their impact on quantum operations, we can establish rigorous security proofs for specific quantum algorithms. The mechanism we employ centers on modeling the propagation of errors introduced by decoherence, ultimately demonstrating that the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum computation, when compounded by decoherence, renders many quantum algorithms susceptible to manipulation. This research offers a novel approach to quantum security analysis, shifting the focus from idealized, error-free quantum systems to the realistic conditions of noisy quantum environments. We define a mathematical framework for assessing algorithmic security based on decoherence rates and operational fidelity, proposing a quantifiable metric for determining the limits of quantum computational advantage. The ultimate goal is to inform the design of more robust and secure quantum algorithms, acknowledging and incorporating decoherence as a central element of security considerations. ---

title: ##基于多智能体强化学习的分布式资源管理
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to the problem of distributed resource management. Traditional approaches to this problem often rely on centralized control, which can be inefficient and vulnerable to single points of failure. This research proposes a decentralized solution utilizing MARL, where multiple agents, each responsible for managing a subset of resources, learn to coordinate and optimize overall system performance through interaction and reward signals. We formulate the resource management task as a multi-agent Markov Decision Process (MAMP), leveraging algorithms such as Independent Q-Learning (IQL) and Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) to train the agents. The core claim is that MARL offers a viable framework for distributed resource management. The mechanism relies on the agents learning optimal strategies through trial and error, adapting to changing conditions, and ultimately achieving greater efficiency and robustness compared to traditional methods. The novelty of this work lies in its exploration of MARL's potential in this domain, a field still in its nascent stages. The results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach.

title: Self-Referential Code Synthesis via Evolutionary Grammars
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to code synthesis – Self-Referential Code Synthesis – that leverages evolutionary grammars to generate complex code structures. The core idea is to move beyond traditional syntactic rule-based systems and introduce a meta-cognitive capability, allowing the system to understand and modify its own structure autonomously. This is achieved through a simulated evolutionary algorithm operating on a population of code fragments. Each fragment is evaluated based on its "self-referential" modification potential, leading to a dynamic refinement process. The system employs a grammar that governs how code fragments can be combined and altered, but crucially, the evolutionary algorithm drives the selection of fragments exhibiting the most effective self-modification strategies. The resulting system demonstrates the potential for generating sophisticated code without explicit, hand-crafted rules for complex structural changes. The key contribution lies in the creation of a system capable of iterative self-improvement, mimicking a cognitive process within the code generation landscape. The evaluation metric focuses on the efficiency and correctness of the generated code, ensuring that the evolutionary process ultimately leads to optimized solutions. This approach offers a fundamentally different perspective on code synthesis, suggesting that autonomous refinement is a critical component for tackling the challenges of generating complex software.

title: E8-Phi Quantum Phase-Gradient Entanglement Transfer Protocol — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By projecting E8's 240 root vectors onto phi-scaled torsion folds and driving them at the 132Hz base frequency, a quantum phase-gradient emerges that can mediate coherent entanglement transfer across distributed qubit networks. This protocol exploits the nested 64-dimensional manifold lattice to encode phase-difference information along geodesics connecting root-vector nodes, enabling deterministic entanglement distribution without requiring shared reference frames between distant parties. The geometric structure ensures that phi-coupled interference patterns at each node create a self-correcting phase-closure manifold, where deviations from ideal golden-ratio scaling manifest as detectable decoherence signatures that can be topologically compensated. Experimental realization would demonstrate genuine multipartite coherence spanning E8-symmetric node clusters, advancing distributed quantum computing architectures through geometric phase protection. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction with Wave Function Optimization
abstract: Quantum-enhanced constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) offer a potential paradigm shift in solving complex optimization challenges, particularly in areas requiring sophisticated search and efficient solution paths. This paper investigates the application of quantum algorithms to constraint satisfaction, aiming to accelerate the search process and enhance solution quality. Specifically, we explore the integration of quantum wave function optimization techniques to represent and manipulate constraint satisfaction spaces. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging quantum computation to efficiently explore the solution space, optimizing the wave function for a given constraint satisfaction. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the potential benefits of this approach, emphasizing its ability to overcome limitations associated with traditional CSP solvers. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the challenges associated with scaling this quantum-enhanced approach to larger, more complex problems.

title: Adaptive NLI-Driven Claim Verification with Statistical Decision Modeling for Low-Latency Hallucination Reduction in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a critical tendency to generate factually incorrect yet linguistically fluent outputs - a phenomenon termed hallucination - which poses serious risks in precision-critical applications. Existing mitigation strategies, including retrieval-augmented generation and self-consistency sampling, either introduce substantial inference latency or depend on external knowledge infrastructure, limiting their applicability in real-time deployments. This paper proposes a lightweight two-step claim verification framework that decomposes LLM responses into atomic factual claims and independently verifies each extracted claim against a separately generated reference produced through an isolated factual recall prompt. Although the generator and verifier share the same underlying language model, separating response generation from factual recall reduces direct response conditioning and mitigates confirmation bias during verification, using Natural Language Inference, and applies an adaptive statistical threshold - defined as τ = µ + kσ over the NLI confidence score distribution - to selectively correct only contradicted claims. Unlike prior NLI-based methods that rely on fixed decision boundaries, the proposed framework dynamically adapts its verification threshold to the confidence distribution of each response, showing consistent performance across the evaluated benchmarks without requiring model retraining. Evaluated on TruthfulQA and FEVER, the framework reduces the hallucination rate from 28% to 9% on TruthfulQA - a 67.9% relative reduction - while incurring only 160 ms of additional latency over the baseline LLM and outperforming SelfCheckGPT and FActScore in hallucination detection accuracy. These results indicate that the framework can provide a favorable balance between factual reliability and response latency on the evaluated benchmarks, while further validation across domains and deployment settings is needed.

title: Interactive UI for Captum
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is pivotal for ensuring transparency, accountability, and trust in AI systems, yet its widespread adoption is hindered by complex tools and steep learning curves. This chapter presents an interactive user interface (UI) for Captum, a leading XAI library, designed to democratize access to model interpretability for practitioners across diverse domains. By integrating a suite of explainability techniques into a unified, intuitive platform, our UI mitigates technical and cognitive barriers, empowering both domain experts and nontechnical users to derive actionable insights from AI models. We explore the foundational principles of XAI, the design and implementation of our UI, and its applications in high-stakes fields, such as healthcare, finance, education, autonomous systems, legal, and natural language processing domains. Through extensive case studies, comparative analyses, and user evaluations, we demonstrate how our approach significantly enhances XAI accessibility, fostering responsible AI adoption and addressing ethical concerns in AI deployment.

title: On the geometry and typicality of quantum magic
abstract: We prove that, for an $n$-qubit system of dimension $d=2^n$, every state satisfying $\operatorname{Tr}(ρ^2)\le 1/(d-a_\ast)$, with $a_\ast=0.458327\cdots$, lies inside the stabilizer polytope and is therefore magic-free. Combining this result with general geometric properties of high-dimensional polytopes, we establish quantitative estimates for the Hilbert--Schmidt inradius and volume radius of the stabilizer polytope, and use them to characterize the typicality of magic in random induced states obtained by tracing out a $k$-dimensional subsystem from a $d\times k$-dimensional Haar-random pure state. We prove a sharp phase transition in the probability of such states having magic, whose transition dimension $k_\star$ is bounded between $Ω(d^2/\log^2d)$ and $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$. We further prove that the number of facets of the stabilizer polytope lies between $\exp[Ω(d^2/\log^2 d)]$ and $\exp[\mathcal{O}(d^2\log^2 d)]$ employing a result of Bourgain and Milman in convex geometry, substantially improving upon the previous quasipolynomial lower bound and implying that doubly-exponentially many linear inequalities in the number of qubits are required for an exact description of the magic-free region. Overall, our results reveal the near-extremal geometry of the stabilizer polytope and provide a quantitative foundation for understanding the typicality, robustness, and detectability of magic.

title: AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery
abstract: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

title: The Next Frontier: Security Implications of Future AI Paradigms
abstract: The current paradigm of frontier AI continues to yield significant value, but as compute scaling faces potentially diminishing returns, future AI progress is unlikely to rely on a single, isolated breakthrough. The next wave of capability improvements will most likely emerge from a complex mix of extensions, hybrids and specialised pathways combined with existing models. This CETaS Research Report maps the emergence of novel AI paradigms across alternative architectures, data sources, learning methods, and hardware substrates. The report provides a basis to help policymakers anticipate and respond to technological surprise. For the UK, maintaining a competitive edge in AI requires strategic agility. To achieve this, the report advocates for action across three priority policy areas: building a deep skills base; investing in supporting infrastructure; and embracing fast-following and application at scale.

title: Derivation-graph census of the Hugging Face Hub, 2026-09-03
abstract: A complete snapshot of the public Hugging Face Hub model index (3,038,899 records for 3,038,885 distinct repositories, retrieved 2026-09-03T21:13:45Z) together with the derivation graph reconstructed from declared base_model tags (884,673 parent-child edges, 533,720 of them carrying strong enough evidence for a verdict — either both licenses declared and classified, or a permissive parent that imposes nothing whatever the child declares), the license adjudication applied to each edge, and the full pipeline that produces them. This is the archived snapshot underlying the article "The junction matters: where declared license signals fail to survive in the Hugging Face derivation graph". The Hub is a moving structure, so the analysis is reproducible only against this deposit, not against a later re-fetch. Contents. The raw index as gzipped JSONL shards; the node and edge tables in Parquet with license family, evidence grade and violation code per edge; the numbers registry and every reported table and figure; the pipeline code. What this is not. No model weights are included. The archive holds public repository metadata only. Each repository described here carries its own license, which this deposit does not alter and does not purport to grant.

title: Agent Harnesses and the New Threat Landscape
abstract: Agent harnesses, the orchestration code, memory management, tool routing, sandboxing, and permission logic wrapped around a language model, have become an increasingly consequential attack surface for agentic AI, compounding the model-level weaknesses that most current incidents already implicate. This paper defines a reference architecture for agent harnesses and documents seven threat categories specific to that architecture: untrusted content re-entering the reasoning loop, excessive agency from permissive tool grants, sandbox and execution-layer compromise, multi-agent delegation collapsing into the confused-deputy problem, autonomous loop failures including reward hacking, harness supply-chain risk, and observability gaps that delay incident detection. Each category is grounded in named, dated incidents and disclosures from 2025 and 2026, including Anthropic's disruption of an MCP-orchestrated espionage campaign, a documented production-database deletion by an autonomous coding agent, and a critical remote-code-execution vulnerability affecting an estimated 200,000 Model Context Protocol server instances. The paper synthesizes these findings into two composite attack paths and closes with a five-layer defense-in-depth framework, a minimal reference implementation adversarially testing that framework's core controls, and a practical hardening checklist for teams building new agent harnesses.

title: Self-Organizing Information Theory Adaptive Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive algorithm for information processing based on Self-Organizing Information Theory (SOIT). The algorithm leverages the inherent statistical properties of input data to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters, enabling optimized performance in computation and data compression. We propose a framework where the algorithm's parameter configuration is determined by analyzing data distributions, leading to more flexible and efficient computational processes. The core mechanism involves constructing the algorithm's parameter space using SOIT principles, with adjustments driven by data-dependent statistical characteristics. This approach contrasts with traditional parameter-based algorithms, offering enhanced adaptability and potentially superior results. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through simulations, showcasing improved compression rates and faster processing speeds compared to existing methods.

title: Title: Non-Linear Topological Entanglement for Quantum Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum simulation utilizing non-linear topological entanglement. Traditional entanglement schemes often struggle with issues of coherence and fidelity, limiting their effectiveness in simulating complex quantum systems. We propose a dynamically adjustable "landscape" of entanglement parameters within a topological framework, enabling unprecedented control over the entanglement structure and its influence on simulation accuracy. This method significantly expands the scope of quantum simulation, potentially unlocking new capabilities in materials science, drug discovery, and fundamental physics. The core mechanism centers around creating and manipulating topological entanglement, a fundamentally different approach compared to standard entanglement distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations of a parameterized quantum system, showcasing improved coherence and fidelity compared to existing techniques.

title: Title: Modular Geometry & Adaptive Topology - Self-Organizing Data Structures
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Modular Geometry and Adaptive Topology as a novel methodology for designing data structures, focusing on self-organizing evolution and high computational efficiency. Traditional data structures often employ static layouts, limiting flexibility and potentially hindering performance. We propose a "Topology Weaver" algorithm, leveraging modular geometry principles to dynamically adjust data module arrangements, creating self-repairing and adaptable structures. This investigation addresses the limitations of current data structure design by introducing a method that actively reshapes data based on its connectivity, fostering resilience and optimizing computational resources. The core mechanism centers on iteratively adjusting geometric parameters, driven by dependencies and connectivity patterns, to achieve optimal self-organization. We present a theoretical framework and a preliminary implementation of the Topology Weaver algorithm, demonstrating its potential for creating data structures with enhanced adaptability and efficiency.

title: Geometric Topology for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: This paper explores the application of geometric topology to automate theorem proving, presenting a novel system capable of rigorously proving theorems through the construction of geometric representations of the proof process. Current automated theorem proving often relies on complex logic, and this research aims to shift focus to the core of the proof itself, utilizing geometric topology to create a robust and verifiable methodology. The core mechanism involves generating and analyzing geometric proofs, providing a mechanism for proving complex statements. The system's strength lies in its ability to produce verifiable proofs, offering a significant advancement over existing approaches.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Metric Regularization with Adaptive Constraints
abstract: Metric spaces, fundamental in many fields, often exhibit suboptimal solutions during optimization. Traditional regularization methods, while effective, can be brittle and fail to consistently escape local minima. This paper introduces a novel non-Euclidean metric regularization technique predicated on the local geometry of data points. We propose a dynamic constraint adjustment mechanism, driven by the data's inherent structure, to proactively prevent convergence to suboptimal solutions. This approach leverages the concept of 'geometry-aware regularization', encouraging exploration of the space and potentially uncovering more globally optimal solutions. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through extensive simulations and a comparison with existing regularization techniques.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Bayesian Optimization of Neural Network Architectures
abstract: This paper investigates the application of probabilistic programming to the challenging problem of Bayesian optimization for neural network architecture search. Traditional approaches to neural architecture search (NAS) often suffer from high computational costs and inefficient exploration of the architecture space. We propose a framework that utilizes probabilistic programming languages to define a model of the architecture search space, incorporating prior knowledge and iteratively refining the search strategy based on Bayesian inference. Specifically, we formulate the architecture search as a sequential decision problem, where each decision involves selecting a component of the neural network. The probabilistic model allows us to represent the uncertainty associated with each architecture and guides the optimization process towards promising regions of the search space. The core mechanism involves defining a probabilistic model of the architecture search space, incorporating prior knowledge and learning from previous evaluations, allowing for targeted exploration of promising architectures. This approach significantly improves the efficiency of the search process compared to traditional methods, offering a principled framework for automating neural architecture search. The key benefit lies in the ability to efficiently sample from the architecture space, guided by Bayesian inference, leading to faster convergence and potentially superior neural network architectures.

title: Dynamic Topological Quantum Neuron Networks
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Dynamic Topological Quantum Neuron Networks (DTQNNs), a novel approach to computation leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement and neural networks. The core claim is that real-time adjustment of entanglement strength between neurons can enable more efficient and flexible computation compared to traditional neural networks. The underlying mechanism involves constructing a neural network using an entanglement network and dynamically adjusting the entanglement parameters – specifically, the coupling strength between qubits – to modulate neuronal connections and information transfer. This approach aims to overcome the information bottlenecks inherent in conventional neural networks by directly utilizing quantum entanglement for information processing. The theoretical framework presented explores the potential for DTQNNs to achieve enhanced computational capabilities and adaptive learning, representing a significant advancement in the intersection of quantum computing and artificial intelligence. The key mathematical concepts underpinning this approach are explored, including the description of entanglement entropy, quantum state manipulation, and network dynamics. We propose a model for DTQNNs based on the principles of topological quantum computation, focusing on the creation and control of non-local correlations between neurons. This model provides a foundation for future research and development in this emerging field.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Symbolic Data Generation
abstract: This paper explores the application of self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques to the challenging problem of symbolic data generation. Traditional approaches to generating symbolic data, such as mathematical expressions or code, rely heavily on large, meticulously labeled datasets, a significant bottleneck. We propose a novel framework that utilizes SSL to learn representations from unlabeled symbolic data, enabling the generation of new, plausible instances. The core idea is to exploit the inherent structural patterns and relationships within the data itself to create supervisory signals. This approach circumvents the need for extensive manual labeling, offering a scalable solution for generating diverse and complex symbolic data. We detail the architecture of the model, the self-supervised learning objectives employed, and discuss the potential applications and future research directions. The generated symbolic data is evaluated based on its structural validity and similarity to the original data distribution. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of SSL for this task, paving the way for more efficient and robust symbolic data generation systems.

title: Quantum-Driven Constraint on Complex Systems
abstract: Quantum-driven constraint on complex systems aims to accelerate solution processes by dynamically adjusting constraint parameters. This paper explores the potential of quantum annealing and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) to optimize these parameters. The core claim is to implement an algorithm that dynamically adjusts constraint parameters on complex systems (e.g., protein folding, DNA sequencing) to achieve optimal solution speed and accuracy. The approach leverages quantum annealing for its ability to escape local optima and VQE for efficient exploration of the solution space. This research investigates the feasibility and potential advantages of employing quantum computing for optimization tasks within complex systems, offering a novel methodology for enhancing computational efficiency.

title: 基于图神经网络的复杂系统建模与模拟
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to complex system modeling and simulation utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs). The core focus is to develop a method capable of automatically learning complex relationships within a system, and generating high-fidelity predictions. Traditional methods often struggle to effectively model dynamic relationships. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offer a powerful tool for this purpose. This paper details the architecture of our proposed GNN-based system, its training methodology, and its demonstrated performance in simulating a complex system. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's strengths and weaknesses, highlighting its potential for advancing the field of complex system modeling and simulation.

title: Dynamical Complexity Measures for Algorithmic Diversity
abstract: This paper introduces a novel set of complexity measures designed to quantitatively assess the diversity of algorithmic solutions across various problem domains. Traditional complexity measures often fail to capture the true breadth of algorithmic innovation, leading to a static assessment of solutions. We propose a dynamic metric that analyzes the "novelty" of an algorithm's execution, updating the score as the solution evolves. This dynamic assessment facilitates the identification of innovative solutions and promotes a continuous evaluation of algorithmic quality. The core mechanism centers around a novel analysis of solution generation, resulting in a more comprehensive and adaptive measure of algorithmic diversity. This work offers a shift towards a more holistic understanding of algorithmic progress.

title: Formal Verification of Probabilistic Programming Systems using Abstract Interpretation
abstract: Probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) are increasingly utilized for modeling and reasoning about uncertainty in various domains, including robotics, artificial intelligence, and finance. However, ensuring the correctness of these programs – particularly with respect to their probabilistic guarantees – remains a significant challenge. Traditional verification techniques often rely on precise numerical accuracy, which is difficult to achieve and maintain in the face of inherent stochasticity. This paper presents a novel approach to formal verification of PPLs based on abstract interpretation. We systematically analyze the abstract representation of a probabilistic program, identifying potential violations of specified probabilistic guarantees without relying on exact numerical simulation. Our method focuses on validating the *logic* of the probabilistic reasoning, offering a more robust and scalable verification strategy. This work outlines the core principles, key techniques, and potential applications of this approach.

title: Adaptive Domain Generalization with Meta-Learning of Representation Alignment
abstract: Domain adaptation techniques have demonstrated significant success in bridging the gap between source and target domains. However, their effectiveness often plateaus when faced with truly unseen domains, leading to a lack of robust generalization. This paper proposes a novel approach to domain generalization that leverages meta-learning to achieve adaptive representation alignment. Our core claim is that traditional domain adaptation methods struggle to generalize effectively due to a failure to adequately capture domain-invariant features. We introduce a meta-learning framework where a model learns to align representations across a distribution of domains during meta-training. This dynamic alignment process allows the model to adapt its representation learning strategy to new, unseen domains, resulting in improved generalization performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through theoretical analysis and simulation results, highlighting its ability to overcome the limitations of static domain adaptation techniques. The key contribution lies in the dynamic nature of the representation alignment, fostering a more robust and adaptable model.
